scope: Current name-usage check for the eight article spellings against Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes. This review addresses nomenclature only; it does not re-identify specimens, confirm local occurrence, or verify article statements about native status and introduction year.

catalogOfFishes.publisher: California Academy of Sciences, Institute for Biodiversity Science and Sustainability
catalogOfFishes.versionNote: Online catalog version reviewed 30 October 2026; selected pages display updates through 13 August 2026.
catalogOfFishes.supports: Current valid-name combinations and nomenclatural status only. Catalog name status does not verify the lake study's voucher identifications.

worms.supports: Lists Cyprinus carpio rubrofuscus as accepted under Cyprinus rubrofuscus. This is a name relation, not the identity of the article's koi.

usgsNas.supports: Government comparator describes the domestication/taxonomy complexity around koi and the current use of Cyprinus rubrofuscus; no Philippine locality inference is made.

candidateReviews.conflict: The Lake Danao article calls this species native. The Catalog's distribution note says it is known definitely only from Java and introduced elsewhere. This does not prove the Lake Danao fish was absent or misidentified; it makes the native claim and specimen identity a priority for voucher-level review.

CAS and WoRMS recognize C. rubrofuscus as a valid species; the USGS profile notes that domesticated koi have been assigned different Cyprinus names/subspecies in the literature. The article's common name koi is not sufficient to identify its particular voucher as C. rubrofuscus.

limitations: Catalog of Fishes name status is not specimen identification, and no catalogue numbers for the Lake Danao vouchers were found in the reviewed article text.
Clarias batrachus is the material conflict: article native status versus the Catalog's Java/introduced-elsewhere distribution note. Preserve both claims until qualified voucher and origin review.
Koi domestication and Cyprinus naming remain complex; an accepted name does not independently identify the Lake Danao ornamental fish.
The Oreochromis niloticus year-introduced ambiguity is historical/provenance evidence, not a taxonomic-name conflict, and remains unresolved.
No current fish presence, native status, abundance, diet, bait effectiveness, fishing legality, safety, lake geometry or complete inventory is established.
nextAction: Hold the Lake Danao article's origin and koi specimen-level claims. Seek voucher catalog numbers and a qualified ichthyologist's reading before public app admission; keep source spellings and all article conflicts intact.
